# What the SDK's theme system costs a host app

A trial on Sandsend Retreats (branch `theme-trial`, commit `d19626c`), by an agent acting as the host's developer, using only the public package at v0.7.170, the `ripul_guide` tool and the app's own repository. 11 October 2026, 08:46 to 09:07. The SDK's home repository was not read at any point.

## The answer

- **20 minutes** from the first read to the build running on Peter's iPhone (measured, from the clock). About 10 were the agent working, 8 waiting for builds and screenshots, 2 measuring baselines. These are an agent's minutes: a person would take most of a day, because the work is reading 2,800 lines and editing 12 files.
- **706 lines added, 90 removed, in 27 files** (measured, `git diff main --shortstat`). The app was 1,633 lines of Swift. Only 78 of those lines are what `theming.md` promises a host writes (a token where a system value was).
- **202 of the lines are a script the SDK documents and does not ship**, and without it the View Explorer names no tokens.
- **Nine things the package did not tell me**, listed under "What did not work". Four were found by reading the SDK's source, three by a build or a screenshot going wrong, two are SDK faults that have no cure in the host.
- Release build: 2 seconds faster, 79 KB more code, 1.7 MB more app, nearly all of it fonts (all measured).

## The ledger

Clock times are from `date`, noted at each step. Lines are from `git diff main --numstat` unless marked "counted by hand", which means counted in the diff.

| # | Clock | What and why | Lines, files | Learned from | Should the host do it? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 08:46 to 08:50 | Read `theming.md` (985 lines), the seven files of `ThemeCore/` (1,776 lines), parts of `RipulBaseTokenProvider.swift`. Fetched the website's and install page's styles. | none | theming.md, the source | Reading, yes. Reading the source, no: see 5, 7, 9, 12. |
| 2 | 08:48 to 08:50 | Fonts. The website's are IvyPresto Display and Freight Sans Pro (Adobe Fonts, not allowed in an app). Chose Playfair Display and Source Sans 3, downloaded them with their licences, wrote where they came from. | 4 font files (1,592 KB), 2 licences (186 lines), `SOURCES.md` (14) | the website's CSS; a human decision | Yes. Choosing and licensing a font is the host's. |
| 3 | 08:50 | Wrote the brand document: 8 palette pairs, 9 roles, 2 families. | `sandsend-brand.json`, 28 | theming.md; the install page's CSS for the values | Yes. This is the part that should be the whole job. |
| 4 | 08:50 | Wrote a "default" document that names one thing, `display: system-serif`, so the app's serif headings do not change. | `sandsend-default.json`, 7 | theming.md ("`.serif` has no accessor"), then the source for `system-serif` | No. See "What did not work", 2. |
| 5 | 08:51 | Wrote a rewrite script (16 regular expressions) and ran it: 75 replacements in 9 files. Fonts, hierarchy styles, backgrounds, white and black, sections, the empty state, prominent buttons. | 75 lines changed, 9 files (the script's count); the script itself, 30 lines, is not in the repository | theming.md's tables | No. The SDK has this script and does not ship it. |
| 6 | 08:51 to 08:52 | By hand: three symbols to `ripulIcon` (the script cannot tell an `Image` from a `Text`), the wordmark's fixed size, one section header. | 5 lines changed, 3 files (counted by hand) | theming.md | A tool could, with a parser. |
| 7 | 08:52 | `Brand.navy` and `Brand.cream` become "the theme's accent, once a theme names one": the same idea as the SDK's `ripul(accentOr:)`, for a colour the SDK has no role for. | `Theme.swift`, +6 −11 | the source (`isDefault`, `accentOr`) | No. See 3 below. |
| 8 | 08:52 | Setup: the root modifier, load a document at launch, register the fonts, keep the choice, a picker in the More menu. One `@_exported import` so 12 files need no import line. | `AppTheme.swift` 64, `SandsendRetreatsApp.swift` +2, `StayTab.swift` +10 | theming.md for `adopt` and the root; a guess for `@_exported` (worked) | The root and one line naming the document, yes. The other 70 lines, no. |
| 9 | 08:52 to 08:53 | Wrote `theme_usage_map.py`, which a Debug build runs to write `ripul-theme-usage.json`, from the JSON keys the SDK's reader looks for. | 202 lines; `project.yml` +11 for the build step | the source only (`RipulThemeUsage.swift`) | No. See 1 below. |
| 10 | 08:53 | SDK pin to 0.7.170. First build: compiled first time, no errors. | `project.yml`, 1 line | CLAUDE.md | Yes. |
| 11 | 08:53 to 08:57 | Screenshots of 16 screens, light and dark, before and after, compared pixel for pixel. Found that a text colour set on a page's container (my guess, to avoid step 12) recolours bordered and prominent button labels, list links and section headers. | 4 lines added then removed | a guess that failed | No. See 4 below. |
| 12 | 08:57 | `.foregroundStyle(.ripul(.text))` on each of 29 texts that had no colour, a `Label` taken apart so its text could have one, and a past event's dimming moved from the row to its two texts. | 29 lines added, plus 9 (counted by hand), 10 files | theming.md ("text colours cannot come from a root") | No. This is the largest cost that grows with the app. |
| 13 | 08:57 to 09:02 | Second comparison: all 32 the same as before under the default document. First look at the brand: list rows not themed in dark. | none | screenshots | |
| 14 | 09:02 | Lists: `themedList()` and `themedRows()`, on 2 lists and 6 sections. | `Components.swift` +12, 8 call-site lines (counted by hand) | a guess that half failed (a row background set on the list does nothing), then fixed | No. See 5 below. |
| 15 | 09:02 to 09:05 | Two Debug levers to prove the run-time switch and the explorer's answer with no tap, because nobody is signed in to this app's console. Ran both. | 28 lines, 3 files | the source (`RipulTokenInspector.readout`) | Only as a test. |
| 16 | 09:05 to 09:06 | CLAUDE.md, commit, push, device build (40 s), install, launch with `-theme brand`. | `CLAUDE.md` +20 | CLAUDE.md | Yes. |

### Totals by kind

| Kind | Lines in the repository | Minutes (from the clock, rounded) |
|---|---|---|
| One-off setup (pin, root, load, switch, picker) | 78 | 1 |
| Call-site edits a tool could have made | 80 changed | 1, with a script I had to write |
| Edits that needed a decision (text colour at 29 sites, lists, the brand's two colours, a row's dimming) | 75 added or changed (counted by hand) | 2 |
| Writing the theme document | 28 | 1 |
| Fonts (4 files, licences, sources, registration) | 206 lines of text and 1,592 KB | 2 |
| Build-system changes | 12 | under 1 |
| Workarounds for what the SDK lacks (the map script, the default document for the serif, the levers) | 237 | 2 |
| Lost to something that did not work or was not documented | 4 lines written and removed | 2 |
| Reading before the first edit | none | 4 |
| Waiting for builds and screenshots | none | 8 |

The minutes do not add to exactly 20 because steps overlapped a running build. The line totals are 706 added and 90 removed (measured); the split between kinds is counted by hand from the diff and is right to within a few lines.

### The Release build

All measured: unsigned `Release-iphoneos` builds, clean, same Mac. A control build (the old app, the new SDK) separates the SDK's own growth from the cost of using the theme.

| | Old app, SDK 0.7.169 | Old app, SDK 0.7.170 | Themed app, SDK 0.7.170 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clean build | 206 s | 238 s (fetched the package, and ran beside another build) | 204 s |
| Executable | 60,336,552 bytes | 63,868,632 | 63,947,760 |
| `.app` folder | 71,328 KB | 74,772 KB | 76,472 KB |
| Zipped | 26.2 MB | 27.1 MB | 27.8 MB |

- Using the theme adds 79 KB of code and 1,700 KB of app, of which the fonts are 1,592 KB.
- Moving from 0.7.169 to 0.7.170 adds 3.5 MB of code whether or not the theme is used.
- **What a store build has to worry about.** Before this, the app could have dropped the package from Release (its CLAUDE.md records that as an open choice). Now it cannot: production code calls it, so the whole 60 MB of SDK, its three dependencies and two resource bundles ship to guests in order to read 15 colours and 14 fonts from a JSON file. The theme layer is 1,776 lines; it is not a product of its own. `Package.swift` lists no privacy manifest among the SDK's resources.

### What was checked

- Default document: 16 screens in light and dark, pixel for pixel the same as before the change (measured). One screen differed only by the simulator's own "back to Ripul" mark in the status bar.
- Brand, light and dark: looked at 12 of the 32 screenshots.
- Run-time switch, both ways: a switch 1.5 s after launch against a fresh launch in the same theme. Every pixel of the app's own content the same; the tab bar not (below).
- View Explorer: the SDK's own `RipulTokenInspector.readout(for:)` returned the token lines for `stay.cottage`, `stay.dogs` and `stay.story` (role, value, light and dark, "theme document", the file and line).
- On the phone: installed (`devicectl … info apps`), process running, launched with `-theme brand`, which is kept. A screenshot of the phone timed out twice, so the brand look on the phone itself is not seen by me.

## What did not work

Things the package did not tell me, or told me wrongly.

1. **The three scripts `theming.md` tells you to run are not in the package.** `rewrite_theme_tokens.py`, `check_theme_tokens.py` and `theme_usage_map.py` are given with paths under `ripul-native-app/scripts/`. The package has `tools/publish-theme.mjs` and nothing else. So I wrote my own rewrite (30 lines, thrown away), had no lint, and wrote the usage map generator from the keys `RipulThemeUsage.swift` parses (`k`, `role`, `ctl`, `ctlStyle`, `cond`, `form`, `via` …), which are documented nowhere. The explorer's own message, when the map is missing, tells the host to run "scripts/theme_usage_map.py". Even with the script, `theming.md` says it reads `.uiKitIdentifier(` and `.accessibilityIdentifier(`; this app names controls through its own `.identified(` wrapper, which it would not see. Not tested, since I do not have it.
2. **A serif has no accessor, so "the default document is empty" is false for this app.** Its headings were `.system(…, design: .serif)`. The only way to keep them is a non-empty default document naming `display: system-serif`. That `system-serif` in a family with a weight draws the same pixels as `.system(style, design: .serif, weight:)` is said nowhere; I measured it.
3. **A host cannot add a colour of its own.** The vocabulary is 15 roles, closed. This app has two brand colours that are not the accent under the default look (a fixed navy and a cream). I copied the SDK's `accentOr` idea by hand with `RipulTheme.isDefault`.
4. **Text colour at every site.** `theming.md` says a root cannot carry it and gives the reason. It does not say what to do about the 29 texts that never had a colour, and it does not warn that a container is no better than the root: there, even under the default document, a bordered button's label, a prominent button's label, a list's link and a section header all change colour. Found by screenshot.
5. **Lists are not reached.** A grouped list's ground, rows, separators and header colour stay the system's under a theme that names `surface` and `surfaceSunken`. `Section(themed:)` gives a header the family and not the colour. Nothing in `theming.md` mentions list backgrounds.
6. **The run-time switch and font registration that `theming.md` describes belong to the Ripul app.** `-ripul.theme.document`, `ripul://theme?name=` and `RipulAppTheme.registerFonts()` are not in the SDK. The host writes its own loading, its own persistence, its own switch and its own font registration.
7. **`theming.md` is written for the SDK's own migration, not for a host.** It opens by naming a plan in the home repository, its checks are the home repository's build commands, baselines and "streams". The host's part is twelve lines under "For the theme's owner".
8. **SDK fault: changing back to the default while running leaves the selected tab system blue** until the next launch. The app's accent is an asset colour; the root sets the window's tint to nil when the accent returns to default, and the tab bar does not go back to the asset's colour. Measured by screenshot. No cure in the host that I found.
9. **SDK fault: tab bar labels take the theme's family only after a change while running, not at launch.** At a fresh launch on the brand the labels are the system font; the explorer's readout says so in one breath: "`.AppleSystemUIFont 10 pt`" and "Font set by: the theme". After a live switch they are Source Sans. Measured by screenshot.

Smaller:

- A large navigation title takes the `text` family and the system's colour. A brand whose titles are in its display face, in its ink, cannot say so.
- A document cannot ask for a font feature. Playfair's figures are old-style, so "11:00" on the check-out tile and the dates on What's On look unlike the rest. A theme cannot ask for lining figures.
- `devicectl … launch` needs `--` before the bundle id to pass `-theme brand`; one failed launch. The app's own CLAUDE.md, not the SDK.
- I guessed that `.listRowBackground` on a list reaches its rows. It does not. SwiftUI, not the SDK.

**The forbidden repository was never needed.** Everything missing could be rebuilt from the package's source, at the cost of the 237 workaround lines.

## What the host should have had to do

My view, as the host. Each line is what it should be, then what stops it today.

1. **Add the package and put one modifier on the root.** True today: `.ripulThemeRoot()`, 1 line.
2. **Name a theme file, and nothing else.** `ripulThemeRoot(document: "sandsend-brand")` or a key in Info.plist. Today: 64 lines to find the file, read it, adopt it, keep the choice and fall back.
3. **Put font files in the bundle; the SDK registers what the document names.** Today: the host registers them.
4. **Switch themes with one call that the SDK keeps**, `RipulTheme.select("brand")`, with the launch argument and the URL that `theming.md` already describes working in any host. Today those exist only in the Ripul app.
5. **Run one command to migrate call sites, and one to check.** `swift package plugin` or a script in `tools/`. Today: the scripts are in another repository. This alone was 80 of my lines by a script of my own, and it would have caught the three `Image` fonts.
6. **Nothing at all for the View Explorer.** The package should bring the map generator as a build-tool plugin, and it should follow a host's identifier wrapper. Today: 202 lines and a build step.
7. **No edit for text that has no colour.** This needs the SDK to find a way: a `Text` wrapper, a container modifier that leaves controls alone, or an honest statement that every text needs a line, with the migration script adding it. Today: 29 hand edits, and every new `Text` forgets it silently.
8. **Lists themed by the root, or by one modifier the SDK ships.** Today: two helpers of my own on 2 lists and 6 sections.
9. **A design for a family** (`"display": "system-serif"` is there, but say it draws the same as `design: .serif`), and a way to name the host's own few colours in the same document, read with the same accessor. Today: a second document and a hand-made `accentOr`.
10. **A theme layer the host can link without the agent.** A `RipulTheme` product beside `RipulCommands` in `Package.swift`, with no dependencies. Today a guest's phone carries 60 MB of developer tooling to colour a holiday guide.
11. **A page of `theming.md` for hosts**, starting from "add the package", with none of the home repository's paths.

With those, this trial would have been: the pin, one root line, one document, four font files and their licences, and a migration command. About 30 lines of the host's own, against 706.

## Not measured

- The brand on the phone's own screen. The bridge's screenshot timed out twice. Installed, running and launched on the brand are measured; what it looks like there is taken from the simulator.
- The View Explorer's Appearance section as a person sees it, by selecting an element. Nobody is signed in to this app's console, so I called the function the explorer calls. The map generator's `ctl` and `cond` marks are untested beyond three rows.
- An archive, an export, TestFlight or App Store validation of a build that now links the SDK in production. Launch time and memory with the SDK loaded.
- Dynamic Type at any size but the default, Increased Contrast, right-to-left, VoiceOver.
- The 20 brand screenshots I did not open, the photo gallery under the brand, and onboarding's arrival step in dark.
- Whether the SDK's own `theme_usage_map.py` would read this app's `.identified(` wrapper.
- A person's time. Every minute here is an agent's.
- Whether the rights to the two fonts' Reserved Font Names matter for renamed files: the files are unmodified, only their file names changed.

## The SDK's response

Written by the agent that changed the SDK, 11 October 2026, after the first trial and before the second. Released as SDK 0.7.171 (commits `a3df64632` and `62420e493`). Everything marked measured was run; everything else is said to be reasoned.

### What this tranche took off the host

Each line is what the host does now, against what Sandsend did in the morning. The morning's figures are the ledger's above. "Now" was measured by taking the morning's branch in a throwaway copy under `/tmp`, pointing it at the changed SDK and deleting what the SDK now does: **8 lines added, 283 removed** (`git diff --shortstat`), and it built and ran in the simulator in all four states (each theme at launch, and each switch while running).

| | The morning, on 0.7.170 | Now, on 0.7.171 |
|---|---|---|
| **A theme by name** (items 2 and 4) | 76 lines: a 64-line loader, 2 in the app, 10 for a picker | 1 line, `.ripulThemeRoot(theme: "<name>")` (or the Info.plist key `RipulTheme`), and 1 line for a picker, `RipulThemePicker("Look")`. The SDK finds the document, adopts it, keeps the choice, falls back, and switches with `RipulTheme.select`. The launch argument `-ripul.theme.document` and the link `<scheme>://theme?name=` work in any host; the link in Debug builds only. |
| **Fonts** (item 3) | registration code, about 5 of the 64 lines | 0 lines. Files in the bundle; the SDK registers those whose family a document names. The files and their licences are still the host's. |
| **The tools** (items 5 and 6) | a 30-line rewrite written and thrown away, a 202-line map generator written from the SDK's source, 11 lines of build setup, no check and no lint | 0 lines of script. `tools/ripul-theme` in the package: `migrate`, `check`, `lint`, `usage-map`. The map is one Run Script line and follows a host's own identifier modifier, found and not declared (measured: `.identified(` in Sandsend, and `.cmsInspectorID(` in Ripul's own source, which the old script had missed: 23 more identifiers). `migrate` now also does wrapped system colours and prominent buttons, and with `--named` the named colours. |
| **The two tab bar faults** (8 and 9 under "What did not work") | no cure in the host | Fixed in the SDK and measured by screenshot on iOS 27.0. The first was wider than reported: after a themed accent the whole window went system blue, not only the tab. The root now puts back the colour the app's asset catalogue names. Tab labels take the family at launch. Under the default document the screen is the same pixel for pixel as before the fix, the clock apart. |
| **A page for hosts** (item 11) | 985 lines of `theming.md` written for this repository, and 1,776 lines of source | `docs/theming-for-hosts.md`, 385 lines, from "add the package", with none of this repository's paths. It says that `system-serif` draws what `design: .serif` draws, what the migration leaves for a person, and what is not built. The `sdk` guide of `ripul_guide` points to it. |

Ripul's own app is the proof for the first two: `ripul-native-app/iOS/RipulAppTheme.swift` (64 lines) is deleted, and the app names its document in one call. Its build step for the usage map went from five lines to the one line any host writes.

### What was checked

- SDK builds for the iOS simulator (the `--triple` form) and for macOS. 51 theme tests pass, 12 of them new (the loader, the kept choice, the fallbacks, the link, font registration). 4 tests of the tools on a small app that is not Ripul's.
- `check_theme_tokens.py` reads zero, the lint passes on the diff, the private-function check is clean, Ripul's app compiles.
- Ripul's usage map: the same as the old script's but for the 23 identifiers the wrapper search added (compared as JSON).
- Reference screens under the default document, 56 captures against `~/.ripul/theme-reference/baseline`: none differs in a way this change could cause. Twelve differ: a spinner, a busy row and the start chooser (animated, and marked so by the tool); the session list's right-hand column and the lozenge list, which differ in the same places between yesterday's own captures; and one explorer screen whose inspector panel sat in a different place on a fresh install. I looked at each.
- WAC compiles against the local SDK (a throwaway worktree under `/tmp`, removed).

Not checked: Mac Catalyst, iOS 17, a store build, and the font registration on a phone before the second trial runs it.

### What a host still pays, and four proposals

These were left out because each is a design decision. For each: the proposal I would make, its cost in my own working time (an agent's, reasoned from the size of the code, not measured), and its risk.

**1. A theme layer a host can link without the rest (item 10).**
Proposal: a `RipulTheme` library product in `Package.swift`, with no dependencies, holding `ThemeCore/`; `RipulAgent` re-exports it, so nothing a host or WAC writes today changes.
Cost: about half a day. Eight files move; the usage-map reader and the root have a few reaches into the rest of the SDK to cut (the legacy refresh environment key, the token provider stays behind).
Risk: Xcode links a package product into every configuration, so Sandsend gets the saving only if nothing in its Release build imports `RipulAgent`; today its console is already Debug-only, so it would. The Release app would lose about 60 MB (reasoned from the first trial's measurement, not built). A module rename can break a host that spells a type `RipulAgent.RipulTheme`; none of ours does.

**2. A host's own colours in the document (item 9).**
Proposal: a host declares its roles once in code, each with the colour it is today (`static let navy = RipulHostRole("navy", default: …)`), reads them with the same accessors (`.ripul(.navy)`), and names them in the same document under `roles`. The default is today's value, so the rule that nothing changes holds. The check, the lint and the usage map learn the declared names.
Cost: about a day, most of it the three tools and the tests.
Risk: two role types behind one accessor name can make `.ripul(.x)` ambiguous to the compiler where a host picks a name the SDK also uses; the alternative, turning the fixed enum into an open type, is cleaner to read and touches every `switch` over roles in the SDK. This is also the first step of moving WAC off the legacy engine, so its shape should be chosen with that in mind.

**3. Text that has no colour of its own (item 7).**
Proposal: do not look for a root-level cure; it was measured not to exist. Make it mechanical instead: `migrate` adds `.foregroundStyle(.ripul(.text))` to every `Text` with no foreground in its chain, and `check` counts a bare `Text` so a new one fails the build.
Cost: about half a day, plus a measurement pass in each container (a button, a link, a list row, a toolbar) to prove the added line is an identity there.
Risk: the tool reads text, not types, so a `Text` built in a helper is missed, and inside a control an explicit text role is drawn as the control's tint, which is right today and may surprise under a theme. It is still a line a text; it stops being a line a person writes.

**4. Lists (item 8).**
Proposal: first spend two hours measuring whether a root can do it at all: `scrollContentBackground(.hidden)` set at the root reaches the lists below it, but a row's background set from outside a list does not (the first trial found that). If the root can carry the ground and UIKit's appearance can carry the rows, lists are themed with no edit. If not, one modifier, `.ripulThemedList()`, that `migrate` adds to each `List` and `Form`, with the rows' background applied by the SDK's `Section(themed:)`.
Cost: two hours to know, then half a day either way.
Risk: the system's grouped look has parts no public setting reaches on iOS 26 and later (the inset card's shape and its selected state); a themed row background may lose the system's highlight. Under the default document it must stay the system's own, which a modifier that does nothing until a theme names `surface` guarantees.

Also still the host's, with no proposal here: a font feature in the document (lining figures), the colour of a large navigation title and of a section header, and a way to keep a serif without a second document.

## Third trial: no change to the host's source

Sandsend Retreats' `main` in a throwaway copy (`/tmp/sandsend-zero`, removed), against the SDK in this repository at commit `b09493db9` (not released). 11 October 2026. Xcode 27.1 (27A9269), Swift 6.4, XcodeGen 2.45.3, iPhone 18 Pro simulator on iOS 27.0. Every figure is marked measured or reasoned.

Peter's question: "Is there any way to do this without us changing the host's source code?"

- **Yes, it works.** Sandsend builds and runs themed with not one line of Swift added or changed (measured: `git status` shows `project.yml` and new files only). Under the system look all 36 screenshots match the untouched app: 34 pixel for pixel, and the 2 of the photo gallery differ only where two captures of one build differ.
- **What the host does: 3 lines of project settings and 8 new files.** The plug-in on the app target (3 lines of `project.yml`), one theme document (28 lines), four font files, two licences and a note. No root line, no Info.plist key, no build phase, no script. The pin line changes as for any SDK release.
- **What would stop me recommending it as the only route:** it rests on how the Swift compiler chooses between two declarations of one name, which the language does not promise; and it reaches less than the migration does, on this app most visibly the two lists, which stay the system's black and grey in dark beside navy pages.

My recommendation: make this the way a host starts, and keep `migrate` for a host that wants the rest.

### What was built

All in the SDK, opt-in. A host that does not switch the plug-in on gets none of it.

- **A build-tool plug-in, `RipulThemeRedirect`** (`Package.swift`, `Plugins/RipulThemeRedirect/plugin.swift`). On every build it runs `tools/ripul-theme redirect`, which writes one Swift file into the build folder; Xcode compiles that file into the host's own module.
- **The generated file** (`tools/redirect/RipulThemeRedirect.swift.txt`, 140 lines) declares SwiftUI's names again: the 11 text styles, `Font.system(size:weight:design:)` and `Font.system(_:design:weight:)`, `Font.weight`, `bold` and `italic`, `Image.font`, `Color.red` and four more hues, `Color.primary` and `.secondary`, `Color(UIColor)`, `foregroundStyle` for the hierarchy styles on `View` and `Text`, and `WindowGroup`. Each is one call into the SDK.
- **`ThemeCore/RipulThemeRedirect.swift`** (203 lines) is where each call lands and where everything is decided. With no theme each returns the call site's own value, itself (7 tests).
- **The root with no line written.** The generated `WindowGroup` wraps the host's content in the theme root and installs the theme: the one Info.plist names, or the bundle's only theme document when it names none.
- **A serif with no second document.** `design: .serif` becomes the display family once a theme names one and is the system's serif until then. Both earlier trials needed a 7-line "standard" document for this.
- **The View Explorer's map with no build phase.** The generator reads the unedited source as the migration would have left it and puts the map in the generated file, inside `#if DEBUG`.
- **A name the host already declares is left out** of the generated file, so the host's own is used.

### What broke, and the edges

Each of these was measured in the real app's build, in scratch files that were removed before the measured build.

| Edge | Result |
|---|---|
| Does Xcode compile a plug-in's generated Swift into an app target, and does XcodeGen express it? | Yes to both. `buildToolPlugins` in `project.yml`; the file lands in `build/Build/Intermediates.noindex/BuildToolPluginIntermediates/`. |
| What the host must allow | With the SDK as a local path, nothing: the build ran without `-skipPackagePluginValidation`. For a released package Xcode asks "Trust & Enable" once and `xcodebuild` needs that flag. **Not measured**, because the SDK was not released. It means Sandsend's ship script and the commands in its CLAUDE.md would each gain that flag. |
| The plug-in's sandbox | `/usr/bin/python3` runs inside it and reads the host's sources. |
| `.font(.body)`, `Font.body`, `SwiftUI.Font.body`, in an array, in a ternary, in generic code | All call the generated declaration (read from the object file's symbols). Even the name qualified with `SwiftUI.` is redirected, so a host has no spelling that means "the system's". |
| A redeclared generic method | **Did not work as the probes suggested.** `foregroundStyle<S: ShapeStyle>` and `Image.font(_: Font?)` made every use ambiguous and the app did not compile: SwiftUI's return an opaque type, so the two signatures are never the same. They are now declared as closer matches instead (`foregroundStyle(_: HierarchicalShapeStyle)`, `Image.font(_: Font)`). So the design leans on two compiler behaviours, not one. |
| A hierarchy style given to `fill`, `stroke` or `background` | Not redirected. Only `foregroundStyle` is. |
| A host with its own `extension Font { static var caption }` or `Color.red` | A compile error, "invalid redeclaration", naming the generated file, until the generator learned to leave such names out. Now it builds and the host's own is used. The generator reads text; a declaration it cannot see is still that error. |
| A host type named `WindowGroup`, `WindowGroup(for:)`, a UIKit app delegate | The first is left out by the generator (tested in the tool's tests, not in the app). The other two are not covered: the host adds a flag and writes the root line. |
| A second module | A framework target with the plug-in switched on built and was redirected, in Swift 6 language mode. A target without the plug-in is untouched. |
| Previews | A `#Preview` compiled. Not run in Xcode's canvas. |
| Release and Debug | Both build. The usage map is in Debug only. |
| Incremental builds | A host file that gains a clashing name is picked up on the next build (5 s); the generated file changes and the app recompiles. |
| Two theme documents and no name | The system look, and a line in the log saying to add the Info.plist key (met by accident, when I added a second document for the symbol test). |
| A value equal but not identical | The SDK's new test caught one: `design: .default` was returned as `design: nil`. Fixed before the pixel comparison. |

**Is the rule promised?** No. That a module's own declaration is preferred to an imported one with the same name and type is how the compiler's name lookup behaves, and I know of nothing in The Swift Programming Language or an accepted proposal that states it. The closer-match rule (a non-generic or non-optional parameter is preferred) is ordinary overload ranking and is equally unwritten. Tested with Swift 6.4 only, in Swift 5 and Swift 6 language modes. If a release changed either, the likely failure is loud (an ambiguity error in the host's files) and the cure is to switch the plug-in off; the less likely one is silent, the host going back to the system look.

Mine, not the design's: a first screenshot pass was blank because captures were taken before a slow launch finished; and two build logs were lost to a filter that closed the pipe.

| Fails how | Loudly at compile time, or (a compiler change) silently unthemed | A missed site is silently the system's |

They mix: a migrated file calls the accessors directly and the rest goes through the generated file. So the plug-in can be the start and the migration the finish, a file at a time.

### On the phone: not installed

**The build is made and signed (`/tmp/sz-device.app`, measured) and is not on Peter's iPhone.** From 10:40 until I stopped, CoreDevice listed the phone as unavailable and the bridge reported it "waiting_for_listener", not reachable; I checked five times, the last at the end. The install page route was not used: it ships committed work from Sandsend's own repository, which this trial was not to touch. When the phone is reachable: `xcrun devicectl device install app --device 00008150-001C544E0EBA401C /tmp/sz-device.app`, then launch `io.ripul.sandsendretreats`. It opens on the brand with no argument, because the brand is the bundle's only theme document. `/tmp` does not survive a restart of the Mac.

### What was checked in the SDK

All measured: 56 theme tests pass (5 new on macOS; 2 more are iOS-only and were compiled, not run); 7 tests of the tools pass (3 new); the SDK builds for macOS and for the iOS simulator with the `--triple` form; `check_theme_tokens.py` on Ripul's own sources reads zero; the private-function check is clean; Ripul's app compiles for the simulator (`BUILD SUCCEEDED`; the log also carried "Could not archive SSU artifacts", which I did not look into).

### Not tested

- **A released package:** the trust prompt in Xcode, and `-skipPackagePluginValidation` on the command line. This is the first thing the blind trial will meet.
- Xcode's own interface: adding the plug-in by clicking, and the previews canvas.
- A plain Swift package as the host (the plug-in's code for it compiles and was never run).
- WAC against this SDK. The change adds files and one fallback line in `RipulBaseTokenProvider`; reasoned, not built.
- Mac Catalyst, iOS 17 and 26, Dynamic Type, Increased Contrast, right-to-left.
- A switch of theme while the zero-edit app runs, and the picker. Reasoned to work as in the second trial, since the same accessors are read in the same bodies.
- A large host: the generator reads every Swift file of the target on every build. On Sandsend's 16 files it is not measurable.
- The named hues drawn on screen, and the third `Image` font.
- 26 of the 36 brand screenshots, which I did not open.
- Any Swift version but 6.4, and the `MemberImportVisibility` upcoming feature.
- A person's time. An agent's was about two hours, most of it building the plug-in and waiting for a loaded Mac.

## Fourth trial: from the starting prompt, on the released SDK

- **It works from one tap.** An agent given only the starter's words and the website's address read the `theming` guide three seconds in, and 27 minutes later Sandsend was on the website's colours with not one line of Swift changed (measured: `git diff main` is 5 files, 56 lines added, 5 removed, no `.swift` file).
- **The trust step did not stop it.** It never met the failure: the guide named the flag, so its first build with the plug-in from the released package already carried `-skipPackagePluginValidation` and succeeded. It then wrote the flag into the ship script, the README and the app's CLAUDE.md unasked.
- **What it did not deliver: the fonts, and a dark mode fit to ship.** It asked a person which stand-in font to use, nobody answered in four minutes, and it bundled none. Three navy buttons vanish on the navy dark ground. Both are faults of the guide, and both are fixed in it.

Sandsend Retreats, a clean copy of `main` at `030186d` in `/tmp/sandsend-starter`, branch `theme` (commits `01fb9b7` and `3a7a51f`, not pushed). The public package at v0.7.172 and web build `mv3qz97a`. 11 October 2026, 12:36:53 to 13:04:25. The agent was a new Claude chat ("Sandsend: theme it from the starter") whose whole task was the text the starter "Start with no change to the source" puts in the composer, and one sentence: "The look to follow is the app's website, www.sandsendretreats.com." Everything below is measured from its branch, its files and its transcript, not from its reply, except where marked.

### What it did, by the clock

| Clock | What | Measured from |
|---|---|---|
| 12:36:53 | Started. | the spawn call |
| 12:36:58 | Read the `theming` guide. Then `trains`, `session` and `devices`. | transcript |
| 12:37:05 | Made the branch `theme`. Read the app's theme file, routes and project file. | transcript, git |
| 12:38:16 | Cloned the public package to `/tmp` for the tools, as the guide says. Ran `migrate --dry-run --named` (55 lines) and counted by search what no level reaches. | transcript |
| 12:38:30 | Fetched the website's stylesheet and six of its pages. | transcript |
| 12:39 to 12:46 | Built the untouched app, made a simulator of its own, captured 19 screens in light and dark, twice. | transcript |
| 12:42:20 | Asked a person which stand-in to use for the site's two Adobe fonts, with three choices. No answer; the question lapsed at 12:46:51. | transcript |
| 12:47:07 | Moved the pin from 0.7.169 to 0.7.172 and switched the plug-in on: 7 lines of `project.yml`, 4 of them a comment. | git |
| 12:48:36 | First build with the plug-in: succeeded, with the flag. | transcript |
| 12:52 to 12:55 | Compared the plug-in build, with no document, against both baseline sets. One new difference, on the Story screen: the Dynamic Island had appeared in a capture. Captured again; gone. | transcript |
| 12:55:01 | First commit. Wrote the theme document from the site's palette and built. | git |
| 12:55 to 13:03 | Captured the themed app, and the themed build launched with `-ripul.theme.document system`. Built Release. | transcript |
| 13:04:00 | Second commit. Stopped and asked which level next, as the guide requires. | git, transcript |

64 tool calls. Of the 27.5 minutes, about 4.5 were waiting for a person and about 12 were builds and screenshot passes (my estimate from the marks above).

### Against the third trial

| | Third trial (an agent that had built the plug-in) | Fourth (a customer's agent, the starter only) |
|---|---|---|
| Swift lines changed | 0 | 0 |
| Diff | 230 lines in 9 files, 199 of them font licences and a note | 56 added, 5 removed, in 5 files |
| Project settings | 3 lines | 3 lines, and 4 of comment |
| Theme document | 28 lines, copied from the second trial | 33 lines, written from the website's own stylesheet |
| Fonts | 4 files, copied from the second trial | none: see below |
| Package | a local path, so no trust step | released v0.7.172, with the flag from the first build |
| The flag written into the repository's commands | not needed | the ship script, the README and two commands in CLAUDE.md |
| Screens compared under the system look | 36, baseline captured once | 38, baseline captured twice |
| Time | about two hours, most of it building the plug-in | 27.5 minutes |

### The five questions

1. **Did it find and read the guide?** Yes, first, before it looked at any file. The starter's words name it.
2. **Did it reach a themed app with no Swift changed?** Yes. I opened its contact sheets: paper and navy in light, navy and sand in dark, the cards, the accent and the tab bar all follow. Body text is black in light and white in dark, and the two lists are the system's, as level 1 leaves them. It said so and named the screens.
3. **Did it meet the trust step and get past it?** It got past it without meeting it. Separately, before the release, I measured the failure itself on a versioned copy of the package: without the flag the build stops with `Validate plug-in “RipulThemeRedirect” in package “…”` and no other explanation; with it the build succeeds. In Xcode's own window the step is a prompt, which was not tested.
4. **Did anything in the guide mislead it?** Three things, below.
5. **Did it prove nothing moved?** Mostly. Of 38 screens, 27 matched the baseline exactly with the plug-in on and no document, and 23 with the document present and the system look asked for. Every difference was in the tab bar, a glass toolbar button, the home indicator or the Dynamic Island, and none in the app's own content. For three light screens it could not match the difference to one in its baseline pair, and called it the system's by reasoning; it said so.

### What misled it, and what I changed

Each change is in the skill file and so in the guide, which is the same text. The guide is live with web build `mv3s73hm` (measured: the live file is byte for byte the repository's), and the skill file is in the public package from v0.7.173 (measured: the tag's file is the repository's). The changed guide has not been run by a fresh agent.

1. **Fonts.** The guide said to propose a stand-in and "let the person decide". It asked, nobody answered, and it bundled nothing, so the most visible part of the brand is missing. Now: ask once, and if no answer comes, bundle the proposed open-licence font in a commit of its own, so it can be dropped, and list it as a decision still open.
2. **How much two captures differ.** The guide said a glass control differs "by a thousand or so pixels". On this run 12 of 38 screens differed between two captures of the untouched app: the tab bar, toolbar buttons, the home indicator, the Dynamic Island. It spent about three minutes on the Story screen before capturing it again. Now the guide says which parts differ, says to record where each difference is and not only whether there is one, and says to capture again before believing a new difference in the status bar or tab bar.
3. **The app's own colours against the theme's ground.** The guide warned about text contrast and said nothing of the app's fixed colours. The agent chose the site's navy for the dark ground, and the app's own navy buttons, which level 1 cannot reach, vanished on it. It caught this in its screenshots and reported it, but only after choosing. Now the guide says to check those colours against the grounds in both modes before settling the values.

Also added: a Mac has no image library, so the guide now says to make a virtual environment with Pillow (the agent found this out and did so, one minute).

Not the guide's: one `ripul_guide` call timed out while the host reloaded, and one search failed on the shell's handling of `*`.

### What I would still not claim

- **A person in Xcode.** The trust prompt, and adding the plug-in by clicking.
- **A project with no generator.** Sandsend uses XcodeGen. The guide tells an agent to ask the person to add the plug-in in Xcode otherwise; not tried.
- **A second agent, or Codex.** One run, one harness.
- **Levels 2 and 3 from a starter.** This run stopped at the question, as it should.
- **That a person would have tapped this row.** The row is in the build; nobody but me has seen it.

### On the phone

**Built and signed, and waiting for the phone.** The trial's branch at `3a7a51f` is at `/tmp/sandsend-starter-device.app` (measured: `BUILD SUCCEEDED`, team C7AA358R56, the theme document in the bundle). Peter's iPhone has been unreachable from the Mac Studio since 10:40, by CoreDevice and by the bridge, and still was at 13:06. `/tmp/sandsend-starter-install.sh` checks each minute for four hours and installs and launches the build when the phone answers; its log is beside it. It replaced the job that was waiting to install the third trial's build. The app opens on the theme with no argument, because the theme is the bundle's only document. It has the website's colours and the system's fonts.

---
name: theme-one-system-going-forward
description: "Peter's decision of 11 Oct 2026: the SDK's new base theme layer (RipulTheme, accessors) is the theme system going forward; the older RipulThemeEngine is legacy that WAC carries; build nothing new on it"
metadata:
  type: project
  scope: repo
  repo: ripul
  scope_also: repo:wac-ios
---

After the theme migration of 10 October 2026 the SDK held two theme systems: the older engine lifted from WAC (`RipulThemeEngine`: a host registers its own vocabulary, UIKit colour tagging, the editing and publishing screens) and the new base layer built for Ripul's SwiftUI app (`RipulTheme` in `ThemeCore/`: fixed roles, accessors, light and dark, fonts, live repaint, the usage map and `RipulBaseTokenProvider`). I told Peter this was the main thing standing between the theme system and being a real SDK value. His decision, 11 October 2026, in the chat "Design alignment": "I don't mind the WAC app carrying a legacy for a while as long as moving forward it is clean."

**Why:** he wants the theme system to be a key value of the SDK. Applying the older engine to our own app was hard because it fits the UIKit, light-only app it came from, so the forward path has to be the layer that fits SwiftUI apps, kept free of the old one.

**How to apply:**
- Build every new theme feature on the base layer only: editing, the explorer, publishing a base document, migration tools.
- Treat `RipulThemeEngine`, its vocabulary registration and its editor screens (`Theme*.swift` outside `ThemeCore/`) as legacy: fixes only, no features, no new dependents. Do not extend the old editor to edit base roles; write the base layer's editor new, reusing only what is already general (hosting, the publish review).
- No bridges from new to old: nothing of the base layer goes into a host's own palette or roles maps, and the reserved `ripul` key in a host document stays unread.
- WAC stays on the legacy engine unchanged until it is moved as its own piece of work. Do not break it, and do not migrate it as a side effect.
- Still open and not built (my reading of what "clean" needs, not his words): a host adding its own roles to the base layer, and shipping the rewrite script, lint, check and usage map with the SDK and without Ripul's file layout.

The decision is recorded as Decision 9 in `docs/plans/theme-aware-codebase.md`. See [[theme-framework-sdk-lift]] for how the older engine got into the SDK, and `ripul-ios-sdk/docs/theming.md` for the base layer's contract.
---
name: Generalizable native theme strategies
description: Automatic text theming must use reusable SDK strategies across apps, with app-wide integration and no WAC-specific element rules
type: feedback
metadata:
  scope: repo
  repo: ripul
---

Peter explicitly confirmed on 2026-09-10 that automatic text theming must be a series of generalizable strategies that work across many apps, not an implementation specific to WAC. The selected WAC HomeCell subtitle is a proving example, not an SDK special case.

Keep the developer contract to one app-wide SDK/theme hook (or a central screen/component adapter where runtime identity is otherwise unavailable). Do not require every label/button to register itself or look up replacement copy. Prefer existing stable accessibility identifiers, stored view properties/outlets, and reusable-row semantic context. Detect ambiguous targeting and explain the missing central integration instead of matching by current text, coordinates, index paths, or hard-coded host class/property names. Tests should exercise unrelated model/view types so portability is demonstrated.
---
name: feedback_sdk_release_from_clean_worktree
description: "Publish an SDK tag from a detached worktree at HEAD when the monorepo SDK tree is dirty with another agent's WIP — never ALLOW_DIRTY=1, never stash"
metadata:
  type: feedback
  scope: repo
  repo: ripul
---

`ripul-ios-sdk/scripts/release-public.sh` refuses a dirty `Sources`/`Package.swift`
tree because rsync copies the WORKING TREE, so another agent's in-flight edits ride
into the public tag (this already shipped an in-flight AgentScreen port as v0.4.14).
In this repo the SDK tree is dirty with foreign work most of the time.

**Do not** reach for `ALLOW_DIRTY=1`, and do not stash. Publish from a clean
detached worktree at the commit you actually want:

```bash
# 1. Stamp + commit the new version in MAIN first — the script's own stamp step
#    would commit to the worktree's detached HEAD and be lost.
sed -i '' 's/^let ripulSDKVersion = ".*"$/let ripulSDKVersion = "X.Y.Z"/' \
  ripul-ios-sdk/Sources/RipulAgent/ViewInspectorOverlay.swift
git commit -m "chore(sdk): stamp ripulSDKVersion X.Y.Z" && git push

# 2. Release from a clean checkout of that commit.
git worktree add --detach /tmp/ripul-sdk-release-X.Y.Z HEAD
cd /tmp/ripul-sdk-release-X.Y.Z/ripul-ios-sdk && bash scripts/release-public.sh X.Y.Z --push
cd - && git worktree remove /tmp/ripul-sdk-release-X.Y.Z --force   # ALWAYS remove it
```

Verify the tag got what you meant, in the public clone (`~/Documents/ripul-ios-sdk`):
`git show vX.Y.Z --name-only` lists your files, and `git show vX.Y.Z:<foreign file>`
fails.

**Why:** it gives the user their change on a public tag without touching, shipping,
or asking about another agent's uncommitted work — the only option that satisfies
both CLAUDE.md rule 4 (never silently work around a foreign dirty tree) and the
release script's concurrency guard. **How to apply:** any "release the SDK" /
"ship WAC against the new SDK" ask where `git status` shows SDK edits you did not
make. `/tmp` already holds ~35 stale ripul worktrees — remove yours when done.
See [[project_wac_ota_deploy_flow]], [[feedback_wac_ship_default_target]].
---
name: feedback_sdk_release_after_all_edits
description: Cut the ripul-ios-sdk tag only AFTER every SDK edit for the change is done — a late edit strands WAC on a tag without it
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 3a38c80e-bb09-43b5-98aa-662a86f4f64a
  modified: 2026-07-28T08:39:43.264Z
  scope: repo
  repo: ripul
  scope_also: repo:wac-ios
---

`release-public.sh vX.Y.Z --push` snapshots the SDK working tree at that moment. Any SDK
edit made *after* the tag — even one that builds clean locally — is NOT in the tag WAC
pins, so WAC fails with `cannot find type 'X' in scope` even though the symbol exists in
the monorepo.

Hit 2026-07-28: released 0.5.40, then made `RipulTokenNode`/`RipulTokenNodeScreen` public
so WAC's scope trees could share the builder. Local SDK build passed (it compiles the
monorepo copy); WAC's build failed against the 0.5.40 tag. Cost a full WAC rebuild cycle.

**Why:** the local `swift build`/`xcodebuild` of the SDK proves nothing about what WAC
sees — WAC resolves the PUBLIC repo at the pinned tag, a separate checkout.

**How to apply:** finish every SDK edit for the change (including access-level widening
discovered while wiring the host) → build SDK → *then* release + bump the pin. If a host
build fails on a missing SDK symbol, check `git log v<pinned>..HEAD -- ripul-ios-sdk/`
before debugging the host. See [[project_wac_consumes_sdk_as_pinned_public_package]].

{"guide":"# Trains: builds and deploys shared between agents

When several agents work on one Mac, their builds and deploys collide: two deploys overwrite each other, a rebuild restarts an app someone is testing, an install lands on a phone mid-test. Trainyard, part of Ripul Host, queues that work. A **track** is one job (a deploy, a build, an install). Agents ask for it; one run serves everyone waiting.

## Does this repository use trains?

It does if it has a file `.ripul/trains.yaml`. Then:

```bash
ripul-train config     # the tracks and resources this repository defines
ripul-train status     # what is running, queued, held and held back
```

Where a repository has tracks, use them. Do not run the underlying build or deploy command yourself, even if you can see it in the file.

## Using a track

```bash
ripul-train request <track> --wait          # board the train and wait for the result
ripul-train hold <resource> --reason "testing sign-in" --ttl 20
ripul-train release <hold-id>               # as soon as the test is done
ripul-train block <commit> --reason "not to ship until the owner says"
ripul-train unblock <block-id>
```

- **Only committed, pushed work ships.** A track normally builds the tip of its branch on the remote, not your working tree. Commit and push first.
- **Take a hold before a test that depends on a shared thing** (the live build, a phone, a running app), and release it straight after. A hold keeps trains that would disturb that thing in the yard. Holds expire: 15 minutes by default, 60 at most.
- **A block stops the whole train**, including other agents' work queued behind that commit. It is for "this must not go live yet", not for routine caution.
- **Disruptive steps wait.** A track can end by restarting or reloading something. Trainyard does that only when the other agents' turns have ended, so the request can take a while to return.
- A repository's own scripts may board a train for you. Its instructions file will say which.

## Setting trains up

A repository without the file has no trains. If its agents are colliding, propose adding `.ripul/trains.yaml` to the user; do not add it unasked. In outline:

```yaml
version: 1
resources:
  staging-site: { kind: manual, description: "The staging site; hold it while testing" }
  dev-server:   { kind: port, port: 3000 }
tracks:
  deploy:
    branch: main
    checks: [ "npm test" ]
```

{"guide":"# Trains: builds and deploys shared between agents

When several agents work on one Mac, their builds and deploys collide: two deploys overwrite each other, a rebuild restarts an app someone is testing, an install lands on a phone mid-test. Trainyard, part of Ripul Host, queues that work. A **track** is one job (a deploy, a build, an install). Agents ask for it; one run serves everyone waiting.

## Does this repository use trains?

It does if it has a file `.ripul/trains.yaml`. Then:

```bash
ripul-train config     # the tracks and resources this repository defines
ripul-train status     # what is running, queued, held and held back
```

Where a repository has tracks, use them. Do not run the underlying build or deploy command yourself, even if you can see it in the file.

## Using a track

```bash
ripul-train request <track> --wait          # board the train and wait for the result
ripul-train hold <resource> --reason "testing sign-in" --ttl 20
ripul-train release <hold-id>               # as soon as the test is done
ripul-train block <commit> --reason "not to ship until the owner says"
ripul-train unblock <block-id>
```

- **Only committed, pushed work ships.** A track normally builds the tip of its branch on the remote, not your working tree. Commit and push first.
- **Take a hold before a test that depends on a shared thing** (the live build, a phone, a running app), and release it straight after. A hold keeps trains that would disturb that thing in the yard. Holds expire: 15 minutes by default, 60 at most.
- **A block stops the whole train**, including other agents' work queued behind that commit. It is for "this must not go live yet", not for routine caution.
- **Disruptive steps wait.** A track can end by restarting or reloading something. Trainyard does that only when the other agents' turns have ended, so the request can take a while to return.
- A repository's own scripts may board a train for you. Its instructions file will say which.

## Setting trains up

A repository without the file has no trains. If its agents are colliding, propose adding `.ripul/trains.yaml` to the user; do not add it unasked. In outline:

```yaml
version: 1
resources:
  staging-site: { kind: manual, description: "The staging site; hold it while testing" }
  dev-server:   { kind: port, port: 3000 }
tracks:
  deploy:
    branch: main
    checks: [ "npm test" ]
    run:    [ "npm run deploy" ]
    verify: [ "curl -fsS https://staging.example.com/health" ]
    disturbs: [ staging-site ]
```

A **resource** is a thing trains affect and agents use. Its kind says how Trainyard knows it is in use: `manual` (only while someone holds it), `port`, `process`, `command` (a probe that succeeds while in use) or `agents` (while any agent is mid-turn). A track lists the resources it disturbs. `ripul-train config` checks the file. The Trainyard screen in the Ripul app edits the same file.
","title":"Trains: builds and deploys shared between agents","topic":"trains"}

content.text:
{"guide":"# Plans

In Ripul a plan is a design document in the repository that can be reviewed: people and agents file comments against its sections, the author answers them, and the fixes become tasks. The user reads and acts on plans in the **Plans** screen of the Ripul apps, where each plan shows as Open or Locked with its comments and tasks. Use this guide when asked to write, review, revise or carry out a plan.

## What a plan is made of

A plan is three files that share a name in `docs/plans/` of the chat's working directory:

- `<slug>.md` is the plan itself, in prose. This is the only file you write by hand, with your normal file tools.
- `<slug>.plan.jsonl` is the log of comments, replies, status changes and tasks. Only the plan tools add to it.
- `<slug>.review.md` is a readable review, rebuilt from the log on every change. Never edit it.

No tool creates a plan. To start one, write `docs/plans/<slug>.md` with a title and `##` sections (the Plans screen starts new plans with Problem, Approach and Open questions). If a file with that name already exists, it is someone's plan: revise it or choose another name.

These are ordinary repository files. The plan tools write to the working directory without asking the user for approval, and they do not commit; commit the files with the rest of your work.

## Which to use: a Ripul plan, or your own plan mode or todo list

When the user asks for a plan, a design or a proposal they will read or have reviewed, write a Ripul plan. Your built-in plan mode and todo list live inside your own session: the user cannot open them in the Plans screen, another agent cannot comment on them, and nothing records what was agreed. Keep your own todo list for private working steps. Work the user should see as owed on a plan goes in with `planTask`.

Plans are not artefacts: the artefact tools do not read or write them. If the user wants a visual summary of a plan, build that separately (see the `artefacts` guide) and keep the Markdown file as the source.

## The tools

| Tool | Use it to |
|---|---|
| `planStatus` | Read a plan's state: section anchors, outstanding comments, open tasks, Open or Locked. Call it first, every time. |
| `planComment` | File a review comment against a section. |
| `planReply` | Discuss a comment without changing its status. |
| `planResolve` | Move a comment to `accepted`, `resolved` or `wontfix`. |
| `planTask` | Record work owed, usually linked to an accepted comment. |
| `planTaskStatus` | Move a task between `open`, `doing`, `done` and `dropped`. |

Each acts on the plan in the working directory of the chat you are running in.

## Statuses and what moves them

**Comments** go one way: `open` to `accepted`, `resolved` or `wontfix`, and `accepted` to `resolved` or `wontfix`. `resolved` and `wontfix` are final and the tool refuses to move a comment back. This stops a later round reopening what an earlier one settled. If there is something new, file a new comment.

**Locked is computed, not set.** A plan is Locked when no `blocking` comment is `open` or `accepted`. You cannot mark a plan done; you can only clear what holds it open. `accepted` still holds it open: agreeing a fix is needed is not confirming it was made.

**Tasks** move freely in both directions. Take them one at a time: `doing` when you start, `done` when the work is finished. Marking a task `done` does not close the comment it came from; the reviewer does that.

**Severity** matters: `blocking` holds the plan open, `should-fix` is a real gap that does not, `nit` is editorial. Use `blocking` only for what would be expensive to find out later.

## Reviewing a plan

1. `planStatus`, to get the anchor list. An anchor is a section's heading turned into a slug. A shortened slug works if it matches exactly one section; an anchor that matches none, or more than one, is refused. Use `__plan__` for a remark about the plan as a whole.
2. `planComment` for each finding, with the defect, why it matters and a proposed fix.
3. On a later round, first check each `accepted` comment against the revised text. Mark it `resolved` if the change answers it; if not, `planReply` and leave it. Then review the plan again for anything new.

## Answering a reviewer's comment

1. `planStatus`, which lists outstanding comments with the hardest first.
2. Where you agree, edit the plan file to fix it, then `planResolve` with `accepted`, and `planTask` with `fromComment` for any work that remains.
3. Where you disagree, `planResolve` with `wontfix` and your reason in `note`. A decline without a reason will be raised again. Use `planReply` to argue the point or ask a question.
4. Do not mark someone else's comment `resolved`. That is the reviewer's confirmation that the fix is real. Sessions started from the Plans screen to draft or address a plan are refused it on comments they did not file. You may resolve a comment you filed yourself.

## Things that go wrong

- **Renaming or removing a heading orphans its comments.** They are kept and listed by `planStatus` as orphaned. When revising, keep existing headings and add subsections instead.
- **`planStatus` lists at most 40 anchors, comments and tasks each**, with long comment bodies cut short and no replies. For the full text and the replies, read `<slug>.review.md`.
","title":"Plans","topic":"plans"}

{"guide":"# Phones, tablets and simulators

You run on the Mac, but the app you are working on often runs on an iPhone, an iPad or a simulator. Use this guide when you need to put a build on a phone, or look at and operate an app running on a device.

## Two families, two different routes

| Family | Reaches the device through | Needs | Sees |
|---|---|---|---|
| `device_…` screen tools | the app itself, over Ripul's relay | the app running in the foreground, built with the Ripul SDK's developer tools | that one app, element by element |
| `host_bridge_…` | Apple's developer tunnel from this Mac, over Tailscale | an iPhone paired with this Mac | the whole phone, as pixels |

They are independent. The bridge can install and launch an app with no Ripul code in it; the screen tools can drive an app in a simulator, which the bridge cannot reach. A typical job uses the bridge to get the build there and the screen tools to test it.

## Choosing the device

Call `device_list_targets` first. It lists each device's handle (for example `iphone-c603`), model, whether it is connected, which tools it offers, and which agent holds it. For a paired iPhone it also gives the name the bridge tools know it by. Check that `inspect_screen` is among a device's tools: without it the device cannot be operated.

A chat has one **working device**: where every `device_…` call acts when it names no `device`. A message from another phone does not move it. `device_set_working_device` moves the chat, and takes the device for this chat alone: other agents' calls to it are refused until you move, pass `release: true`, or go an hour without using it. Release it when the work is done. If the working device is not connected the call fails; nothing falls back to another device.

`host_bridge_…` calls that name no `phone` act on the working device too, and one that would change a phone another agent holds is refused.

## The loop: install, launch, look, tap, verify

1. `host_bridge_status`: is the phone's tunnel active.
2. `host_bridge_run` builds an Xcode project, installs it, checks the installed build and launches it. If you already have a signed `.app`, use `host_bridge_install` (with `launch`). `host_bridge_ship` is not for your project: it builds Ripul's own app.
3. `host_bridge_launch` brings an installed app to the front, or restarts it with `relaunch`.
4. `device_inspect_screen`. Every element comes back with a short handle such as `e7`.
5. `device_tap_element`, `device_type_text`, `device_scroll_element` or `device_set_value`, addressed by that handle.
6. `device_wait_for_element` for the thing that should appear (or, with state `gone`, disappear). It returns the moment the screen matches.
7. `device_inspect_screen` again to confirm, then repeat from 5.

For a simulator, skip the bridge: install and launch with `xcrun simctl`, then start at step 4.

Prefer `device_set_value` for pickers, switches, sliders and segmented controls: it sets the value and fires the app's handler, which is more reliable than operating the control. Use `device_touch` for gestures or an exact point; it takes the window coordinates that inspect reports, and works in debug builds of the app only.

## What inspect can and cannot see

- **Only the app it runs in.** Not the home screen, not another app, not a phone whose app is closed. For those, `host_bridge_screenshot` returns a picture of the whole screen.
- **Only what a person could see.** Views scrolled out of sight, clipped, or covered by something else are left out and counted in `hidden`. Scroll and inspect again, or pass `includeHidden` to see what was left out.
- **Handles expire.** Inspect again after the screen changes.
- An ambiguous tap fails and lists the candidates; nothing is pressed. Narrow it with `within`, `role` or `id` rather than guessing with `nth`.

## What goes wrong

- **The app is in the background.** iOS suspends it, and `device_…` calls go unanswered. Use `host_bridge_launch`, or ask the user to open it.
- **A timeout is not a failure.** When a tap or typing call times out, the action may still have happened: look at the screen before repeating it. Likewise a `host_bridge_install` or `host_bridge_run` call can be cut off while the work carries on: check `host_bridge_projects` for how the last run ended, or inspect the app, before installing again.
- **The phone's network.** A phone accepts a new tunnel only while joined to a Wi-Fi network or to another phone's hotspot, unlocked at least once since it was switched on, with Tailscale connected. On its own cellular connection, or while providing a hotspot itself, it refuses.
- **A phone that was never paired.** Pairing needs the phone plugged into this Mac by USB once, unlocked, with Developer Mode on. Ask the user.
- **Debugging pauses the app.** `host_bridge_debug` attaches LLDB, runs your commands and detaches; the app is stopped while it is attached.

## Recording

`host_record_screen` records a window or a display of the Mac and shows the video in the chat, with a few stills for you to check. That covers a simulator, whose window is on the Mac, but not a physical phone: use `host_bridge_screenshot` before and after instead. It refuses while the Mac's screen is locked, because apps stop drawing behind the lock screen.

## The `device_bridge_…` twins

These are the same bridge tools on another Mac running Ripul Host, for a phone paired with that Mac; pairing is per Mac. Pass `device` for the Mac and `phone` for the phone: these calls do not follow the working device.
","title":"Phones, tablets and simulators","topic":"devices"}

// swift-tools-version: 5.9

import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "RipulAgent",
    platforms: [
        .iOS(.v17),
        .macOS(.v14),
    ],
    products: [
        .library(name: "RipulAgent", targets: ["RipulAgent"]),
        // Command maps: sentence → an app's own actions, via the on-device
        // model and rules. Deliberately dependency-free and separate from
        // RipulAgent, so an app can adopt it without the agent stack — and so
        // nothing Ripul-specific can leak in.
        .library(name: "RipulCommands", targets: ["RipulCommands"]),
        // The theme for a host that changes none of its source: a build-tool plug-in a
        // host switches on for its app target. Opt-in; a host that does not is untouched.
        .plugin(name: "RipulThemeRedirect", targets: ["RipulThemeRedirect"]),
    ],
    dependencies: [
        .package(url: "https://github.com/gonzalezreal/swift-markdown-ui.git", from: "2.4.1"),
        // 0.2.0 added the frame limit the voice orb needs (VoiceModeOverlay.swift).
        .package(url: "https://github.com/ripulio/thinking-orbs-swift.git", from: "0.2.0"),
        .package(url: "https://github.com/appstefan/HighlightSwift.git", from: "1.1.0"),
    ],
    targets: [

            name: "RipulAgent",
            dependencies: [

        .testTarget(
            name: "RipulCommandsTests",
            dependencies: ["RipulCommands"]
        ),
    ]
)
