content.content:
1	---
2	name: theme-an-app
3	description: Give a SwiftUI iPhone or iPad app its own fonts and colours, light and dark, from one theme document, using the RipulAgent Swift package. Use when asked to theme, brand or restyle an app, to make an app follow a website's or a brand's look, to adapt an app's source to theme tokens, or to say what a theme would reach in an app.
4	---
5	
6	# Giving an app a theme
7	
8	A theme here is one JSON document: colours for light and dark, three font families, and sizes and weights. The RipulAgent Swift package reads it and the app's own screens follow it. This is the procedure for doing that in someone's repository. Follow it in order. It needs RipulAgent 0.7.172 or later.
9	
10	Three rules hold throughout:
11	
12	- **With no theme document the app must look exactly as it did.** Every step below keeps that, and you prove it with screenshots before you call the work done.
13	- **Start with the level that changes no source.** Go further only where the person asks for more.
14	- **The tools read text, not Swift.** What they write and what they count is a draft. A build and a screenshot are the proof.
15	- **A question nobody answers is not a reason to stop.** The person may be away. Where a step says to ask, ask once; if no answer comes, take the choice that is easiest to undo, make it in a commit of its own, go on, and list it in the ledger as a decision still open. The one place to stop without an answer is the end of level 1 (step 6): by then the app is themed.
16	
17	## 1. Find out what the app is
18	
19	Read the repository's instructions for agents and its project files before anything else. You need to know:
20	
21	- **Is it a SwiftUI app for iOS?** This works for a SwiftUI app with a deployment target of iOS 17 or later. If the repository is something else (a website, an Android app, a server, a React Native or Flutter app), say so plainly and stop: nothing here applies. A UIKit app can read the theme through `UIColor.ripul(…)` and `UIFont.ripul(…)` by hand, and gets nothing from levels 1 and 3; say that and ask before going on.
22	- **How it is built**: an XcodeGen `project.yml`, a hand-kept `.xcodeproj`, or a Swift package; the scheme; where build output goes; which Xcode.
23	- **Does it link the package already**, and at which version? Look for `ripul-ios-sdk` in `project.yml`, `Package.swift` or `Package.resolved`.
24	- **How a screen is opened without tapping**: launch arguments, deep links, previews. You will need this for screenshots.
25	
26	If the person asked only what a theme would reach, do step 3 and stop: change nothing and report.
27	
28	**Check that your session can do the work**, before you measure anything. It has to write inside `.git` (try `git switch -c theme`, step 2), fetch a package from github.com, and run `xcodebuild` and a simulator. A sandboxed session often can do none of these: Codex in its workspace sandbox cannot write `.git` or reach the network. If one fails, say at once which, and that the chat needs full access (in Ripul, the Codex settings have a Permission Mode, and "Full access" is the one that allows Xcode builds), and stop there. Do not hand back an audit as if it were the work.
29	
30	## 2. Work on a branch
31	
32	Never on the default branch. Make a branch from it (`git switch -c theme`). If the working tree has changes you did not make, say so and ask before going on. Commit as you go, so each level can be kept or dropped by itself.
33	
34	## 3. Measure before you touch anything
35	
36	**Get the tools.** They are in the package, in `tools/`, and need only `python3`. Where the app links the package they are in its checkout: `<derived data>/SourcePackages/checkouts/ripul-ios-sdk/tools/ripul-theme` in an Xcode project, `.build/checkouts/ripul-ios-sdk/tools/ripul-theme` in a Swift package. Where it does not yet, or to look without building: `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/ripulio/ripul-ios-sdk /tmp/ripul-ios-sdk`.
37	
38	**Count what a theme would reach.** Neither command changes a file:
39	
40	```bash
41	ripul-theme check <source folder>                      # every font and colour written at a call site, by kind
42	ripul-theme migrate --dry-run --named <source folder>  # the lines level 3 would rewrite
43	```
44	
45	Then count by search what no level reaches without a decision: `Text(` with no colour of its own, `List` and `Form`, the app's own colours (`Color("…")`, an asset catalogue, a `Brand` type), and UIKit code. Report these beside the tool's counts.
46	
47	**Take the baseline screenshots.** Build the untouched app and capture every screen you can open, in light and in dark (`xcrun simctl ui <simulator> appearance dark`). Fix the clock first (`xcrun simctl status_bar <simulator> override --time 9:41`). Wait for each screen to finish drawing before capturing it. **Capture the whole set twice, and compare the two sets with each other first.** Two captures of one untouched build are not the same picture: on iOS 26 and later the glass tab bar, a glass toolbar button, the home indicator and the Dynamic Island differ from one capture to the next, and an animated screen always does. On one app a third of the screens differed between two captures of the same build. So record, for each screen, where the two sets differ (the box that holds the differing pixels), not only whether they do. Later, a difference inside one of those boxes is the system's, and a difference anywhere in the app's own content is yours.
48	
49	A Mac has no image library for this by itself: make a Python virtual environment under `/tmp` with Pillow, and write a short script that counts differing pixels and prints their bounding box.
50	
51	## 4. Level 1: a theme with no change to the source
52	
53	The package has a build-tool plug-in, `RipulThemeRedirect`. On each build it writes one Swift file into the build folder, and that file is compiled into the app. It declares SwiftUI's own names again (`Font.body`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`, `WindowGroup`), each as one call into the package, so the app's existing code follows the theme. No Swift file of the app changes.
54	
55	1. **Add or move the package** to 0.7.172 or later: `https://github.com/ripulio/ripul-ios-sdk`, product `RipulAgent`, on the app target.
56	2. **Switch the plug-in on for the app target.** In an XcodeGen `project.yml`, under the target:
57	
58	   ```yaml
59	       buildToolPlugins:
60	         - plugin: RipulThemeRedirect
61	           package: RipulAgent      # the name the package has under `packages:`
62	   ```
63	
64	   In a hand-kept Xcode project (a `.xcodeproj` in git, no generator), make both changes of steps 1 and 2 in `project.pbxproj` yourself, in a commit of their own. Do not ask a person to click: it is six objects, and a build proves them. Where the `xcodeproj` Ruby gem is installed (`gem list xcodeproj`), write them with it; otherwise edit the text, giving each new object a 24-character hexadecimal id that the file does not use. The project gains:
65	
66	   - one `XCRemoteSwiftPackageReference`, with `repositoryURL = "https://github.com/ripulio/ripul-ios-sdk";` and `requirement = { kind = upToNextMinorVersion; minimumVersion = 0.7.172; };`, listed in the project object's `packageReferences`;
67	   - two `XCSwiftPackageProductDependency` objects, each with `package =` that reference: one with `productName = RipulAgent;`, one with `productName = "plugin:RipulThemeRedirect";`;
68	   - the first of them in the app target's `packageProductDependencies`, and in a `PBXBuildFile` (`productRef =` it) listed in the target's Frameworks build phase. A target with no `PBXFrameworksBuildPhase` needs one made and added to its `buildPhases`;
69	   - one `PBXTargetDependency` with `productRef =` the plug-in's object, listed in the target's `dependencies`. This is what Xcode shows as Build Phases, "Run Build Tool Plug-ins".
70	
71	   Then `xcodebuild -list -project <project>` must still read the project, and the build of step 4 must pass. Commit the `Package.resolved` the build writes inside the project, if the repository keeps one or has none to compare with.
72	
73	   In a Swift package it is `plugins: [.plugin(name: "RipulThemeRedirect", package: "ripul-ios-sdk")]` on the target (this compiles; it has not been run in a real package host).
74	3. **Allow the plug-in to run.** Xcode refuses a package's plug-in until it is trusted, and the build fails with the one line `Validate plug-in “RipulThemeRedirect” in package “ripul-ios-sdk”`. On the command line add `-skipPackagePluginValidation` to every `xcodebuild` call, and add it to the repository's build scripts and written commands too, or the next agent meets the same failure. In Xcode itself the person is asked once, "Trust & Enable".

---
name: theme-an-app
description: Give a SwiftUI iPhone or iPad app its own fonts and colours, light and dark, from one theme document, using the RipulAgent Swift package. Use when asked to theme, brand or restyle an app, to make an app follow a website's or a brand's look, to adapt an app's source to theme tokens, or to say what a theme would reach in an app.
---

# Giving an app a theme

A theme here is one JSON document: colours for light and dark, three font families, and sizes and weights. The RipulAgent Swift package reads it and the app's own screens follow it. This is the procedure for doing that in someone's repository. Follow it in order. It needs RipulAgent 0.7.172 or later.

Three rules hold throughout:

- **With no theme document the app must look exactly as it did.** Every step below keeps that, and you prove it with screenshots before you call the work done.
- **Start with the level that changes no source.** Go further only where the person asks for more.
- **The tools read text, not Swift.** What they write and what they count is a draft. A build and a screenshot are the proof.
- **A question nobody answers is not a reason to stop.** The person may be away. Where a step says to ask, ask once; if no answer comes, take the choice that is easiest to undo, make it in a commit of its own, go on, and list it in the ledger as a decision still open. The one place to stop without an answer is the end of level 1 (step 6): by then the app is themed.

## 1. Find out what the app is

Read the repository's instructions for agents and its project files before anything else. You need to know:

- **Is it a SwiftUI app for iOS?** This works for a SwiftUI app with a deployment target of iOS 17 or later. If the repository is something else (a website, an Android app, a server, a React Native or Flutter app), say so plainly and stop: nothing here applies. A UIKit app can read the theme through `UIColor.ripul(…)` and `UIFont.ripul(…)` by hand, and gets nothing from levels 1 and 3; say that and ask before going on.
- **How it is built**: an XcodeGen `project.yml`, a hand-kept `.xcodeproj`, or a Swift package; the scheme; where build output goes; which Xcode.
- **Does it link the package already**, and at which version? Look for `ripul-ios-sdk` in `project.yml`, `Package.swift` or `Package.resolved`.
- **How a screen is opened without tapping**: launch arguments, deep links, previews. You will need this for screenshots.

If the person asked only what a theme would reach, do step 3 and stop: change nothing and report.

**Check that your session can do the work**, before you measure anything. It has to write inside `.git` (try `git switch -c theme`, step 2), fetch a package from github.com, and run `xcodebuild` and a simulator. A sandboxed session often can do none of these: Codex in its workspace sandbox cannot write `.git` or reach the network. If one fails, say at once which, and that the chat needs full access (in Ripul, the Codex settings have a Permission Mode, and "Full access" is the one that allows Xcode builds), and stop there. Do not hand back an audit as if it were the work.

## 2. Work on a branch

Never on the default branch. Make a branch from it (`git switch -c theme`). If the working tree has changes you did not make, say so and ask before going on. Commit as you go, so each level can be kept or dropped by itself.

## 3. Measure before you touch anything

**Get the tools.** They are in the package, in `tools/`, and need only `python3`. Where the app links the package they are in its checkout: `<derived data>/SourcePackages/checkouts/ripul-ios-sdk/tools/ripul-theme` in an Xcode project, `.build/checkouts/ripul-ios-sdk/tools/ripul-theme` in a Swift package. Where it does not yet, or to look without building: `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/ripulio/ripul-ios-sdk /tmp/ripul-ios-sdk`.

**Count what a theme would reach.** Neither command changes a file:

```bash
ripul-theme check <source folder>                      # every font and colour written at a call site, by kind
ripul-theme migrate --dry-run --named <source folder>  # the lines level 3 would rewrite
```

Then count by search what no level reaches without a decision: `Text(` with no colour of its own, `List` and `Form`, the app's own colours (`Color("…")`, an asset catalogue, a `Brand` type), and UIKit code. Report these beside the tool's counts.

**Take the baseline screenshots.** Build the untouched app and capture every screen you can open, in light and in dark (`xcrun simctl ui <simulator> appearance dark`). Fix the clock first (`xcrun simctl status_bar <simulator> override --time 9:41`). Wait for each screen to finish drawing before capturing it. **Capture the whole set twice, and compare the two sets with each other first.** Two captures of one untouched build are not the same picture: on iOS 26 and later the glass tab bar, a glass toolbar button, the home indicator and the Dynamic Island differ from one capture to the next, and an animated screen always does. On one app a third of the screens differed between two captures of the same build. So record, for each screen, where the two sets differ (the box that holds the differing pixels), not only whether they do. Later, a difference inside one of those boxes is the system's, and a difference anywhere in the app's own content is yours.

A Mac has no image library for this by itself: make a Python virtual environment under `/tmp` with Pillow, and write a short script that counts differing pixels and prints their bounding box.

## 4. Level 1: a theme with no change to the source

The package has a build-tool plug-in, `RipulThemeRedirect`. On each build it writes one Swift file into the build folder, and that file is compiled into the app. It declares SwiftUI's own names again (`Font.body`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`, `WindowGroup`), each as one call into the package, so the app's existing code follows the theme. No Swift file of the app changes.

1. **Add or move the package** to 0.7.172 or later: `https://github.com/ripulio/ripul-ios-sdk`, product `RipulAgent`, on the app target.
2. **Switch the plug-in on for the app target.** In an XcodeGen `project.yml`, under the target:

   ```yaml
       buildToolPlugins:
         - plugin: RipulThemeRedirect
           package: RipulAgent      # the name the package has under `packages:`
   ```

   In a hand-kept Xcode project (a `.xcodeproj` in git, no generator), make both changes of steps 1 and 2 in `project.pbxproj` yourself, in a commit of their own. Do not ask a person to click: it is six objects, and a build proves them. Where the `xcodeproj` Ruby gem is installed (`gem list xcodeproj`), write them with it; otherwise edit the text, giving each new object a 24-character hexadecimal id that the file does not use. The project gains:

   - one `XCRemoteSwiftPackageReference`, with `repositoryURL = "https://github.com/ripulio/ripul-ios-sdk";` and `requirement = { kind = upToNextMinorVersion; minimumVersion = 0.7.172; };`, listed in the project object's `packageReferences`;
   - two `XCSwiftPackageProductDependency` objects, each with `package =` that reference: one with `productName = RipulAgent;`, one with `productName = "plugin:RipulThemeRedirect";`;

- **Make sure the file reaches the bundle.** A project that lists its files one by one (most hand-kept ones) does not bundle a file because it is in the folder: add the document, and later each font file, to the app target's resources in the project file. Then look inside the built `.app` for them. A theme that does nothing is most often a document that was never copied.
- **With one theme document in the bundle, it is the app's theme** at the next launch. With more than one, name one with the Info.plist key `RipulTheme`, or the app stays on the system look and says so in its log.

**Fonts.** A font may be bundled only if its licence allows embedding in an app. Fonts served by Adobe Fonts, and most fonts a foundry sells for the web, do not allow it. When the brand's font cannot be bundled, say so, propose the nearest font that can (the SIL Open Font Licence allows it), and ask the person once. If no answer comes, do not leave the app on the system's fonts: bundle the font you proposed in a commit of its own, so that it can be dropped, and list it in the ledger as a decision still open. Put the `.ttf` or `.otf` files in the bundle (top level, or a folder named `Fonts`), each font's licence file beside it, and a short note of where each file came from. Write no registration code and no Info.plist entry: the package registers the files a document names. The name in the document is the font's family name ("Source Sans 3"), not its file name. Prefer a variable font: a file with one weight draws that weight whatever is asked.

**Look at it.** Build, and capture the same screens in light and dark. Open the pictures and read them. To see the app without the theme, launch it with `-ripul.theme.document system`; to see another document, pass its name. That argument lasts for one launch.

## 6. Say what level 1 did not reach, and ask

**Stop here and ask.** Show the themed screenshots, list what was not reached, and ask which the person wants: stop at level 1; fix the few places that matter (level 2); or adapt the whole source (level 3). Do not go on unasked.
